name: Red double-decker bus
fact: Red became London's bus colour after the London General Omnibus Company took over the red-painted Vanguard fleet in 1908.
model_hint: Red double-decker bus. Not single-deck buses and not double-deckers in other colours.

name: Black cab
fact: Every licensed driver has to pass the Knowledge of London, a requirement since 1865.
notes: Cabs are not always black; accept the purpose-built taxi shape.
model_hint: Purpose-built London taxi with a TAXI roof sign, in any colour. Not ordinary cars or minicabs, even if they are black.

name: Red telephone box
fact: The classic K6 kiosk was designed in 1935 by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott for King George V's Silver Jubilee, as a smaller version of his 1924 K2.
notes: Accept both K2 and K6; do not ask the model to tell them apart.
model_hint: Red cast-iron telephone kiosk with a domed roof, crowns on the top panels and many small window panes. Accept both K2 and K6; do not try to tell them apart. Not modern glass phone booths or other red objects.

name: Red post box
fact: The royal cypher on the front shows which monarch was on the throne when the box was made, a custom that goes back to the first roadside boxes of Queen Victoria's reign.
notes: Source seen via a staging mirror of The Postal Museum blog; swap in the public URL. Reading the cypher also unlocks the Royal Cyphers set.
model_hint: Red Royal Mail post box of any shape: a freestanding pillar box, a box set into a wall, or a small box on a post or lamp-post. Not red bins, phone boxes, vans or other red objects.

name: Underground roundel
fact: The roundel first appeared on Underground platforms in 1908, as a board showing the station name.
model_hint: TfL roundel with a red ring and a blue bar across it, at an Underground station. Not roundels in other colours and not round logos of other brands.

name: Big Ben
fact: Big Ben is the nickname of the Great Bell inside the clock tower, not of the tower itself. The tower was completed in 1859 and renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012 for Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee.
notes: Wide radius: the tower is photographed from across the river and the bridges.
model_hint: The Elizabeth Tower clock tower of the Houses of Parliament, with its four clock faces and gilded spire, seen close up or from across the river. Not other clock towers, souvenirs or pictures of it.

name: London Eye
fact: The London Eye opened in 2000. It is 135 metres tall and has 32 glass capsules, each representing one of London's boroughs.
notes: Wide radius: the wheel is photographed from far along the river.
model_hint: The London Eye observation wheel on the South Bank with its oval glass capsules, close up or from a distance. Not other Ferris wheels.

name: Tower Bridge
fact: Tower Bridge was completed in 1894. Its Victorian engine rooms powered the bridge lifts for more than 80 years.
notes: Wide radius: the bridge is photographed from both banks and other bridges.
model_hint: Tower Bridge: two Gothic stone towers joined by high walkways, with the road bridge between them. Not London Bridge or other bridges.

name: Buckingham Palace
fact: Buckingham Palace became the monarch's London home when Queen Victoria came to the throne in 1837. It has 775 rooms.
model_hint: The front of Buckingham Palace, often with the Victoria Memorial, the gates or guards in front. Not other palaces or large buildings.

name: Trafalgar Square lions
fact: The four bronze lions at the foot of Nelson's Column were designed by Sir Edwin Landseer and only added in 1867. Their paws were modelled on a cat's.
model_hint: One of the large bronze lions lying at the base of Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square. Not other lion statues.

name: Borough Market
fact: A market took shape at the foot of London Bridge about 1,000 years ago. Borough Market has been on its current site since 1756 and is run by a charitable trust.
model_hint: Borough Market: covered Victorian market halls with green ironwork and glass roofs, food stalls and crowds. Any food market stalls under iron-and-glass roofs; location decides which market.

name: Camden Market
fact: Camden Market opened in 1974 as a small Sunday craft market of 16 stalls behind the Dingwalls music venue. Today it has more than 1,000 shops, stalls, bars and cafés.
model_hint: Camden Market: market stalls, shops with large sculptures on their fronts, the canal lock, the Stables Market or the Camden Lock sign.

name: Columbia Road Flower Market
fact: The flower market runs on Sundays only, from 8am until about 3pm. The Victorian shops along the street were built in the 1860s.
notes: Sundays only; the clue says so.
model_hint: Columbia Road Flower Market: a narrow street of small shopfronts with flower and plant stalls along it.

name: Portobello Road Market
fact: Portobello Road is named after a farm that took its name from the capture of Puerto Bello, in today's Panama, in 1739. The market is famous for its antique and bric-a-brac stalls.
notes: The street is 1.72 km long; the radius covers the market stretch from the centre point.
model_hint: Portobello Road Market: stalls of antiques, bric-a-brac, clothes or food along a street of brightly painted houses.

name: Primrose Hill view
fact: Primrose Hill is 64 metres high, with a clear view of central London from the top. It was once part of a hunting chase taken by Henry VIII, and opened to the public in 1842.
model_hint: The view of the central London skyline from the top of a grassy hill, or the hilltop itself with people on the grass.

name: Greenwich Park and the Royal Observatory
fact: King Charles II ordered the Royal Observatory to be built in 1675. Greenwich became the place that defines zero degrees longitude for the world, and the time ball on the roof was installed in 1833.
notes: Coordinates corrected on 27 Oct 2026 to Flamsteed House on OpenStreetMap: the earlier point (51.477, -0.0147) was about 920 m away, in Greenwich town centre. The park and the outside of the Observatory are free; the meridian courtyard is ticketed.
model_hint: The Royal Observatory Greenwich: the red-brick Flamsteed House with the red time ball on its roof, the Prime Meridian line, or the view from the hill in Greenwich Park over to Canary Wharf.

name: St James's Park pelicans
fact: Pelicans have lived in St James's Park since 1664, when a Russian ambassador gave them to King Charles II. They are fed fish every day at around 2.30pm.
notes: Animals move: wide radius covering the lake.
model_hint: A pelican (large white bird with a long beak and throat pouch) in a park. Not swans, geese or gulls.

name: Richmond Park deer
fact: About 600 red and fallow deer roam Richmond Park. They have lived here since 1637, when Charles I turned the land into a hunting park.
notes: Large park far from the centre. Keep a safe distance from the deer.
model_hint: A red deer or fallow deer in open parkland. Not dogs, horses or statues of deer.

name: Southbank Undercroft
fact: Skateboarders have used the undercroft beneath the Queen Elizabeth Hall since the 1970s, and it is called the birthplace of British skateboarding. When plans to move them were made, the Long Live Southbank campaign gained over 120,000 members and the plans were put on hold.
model_hint: The covered skate space under a concrete building, with graffiti-covered walls and pillars, often with skateboarders.

name: Wembley Stadium
fact: The new Wembley Stadium opened in 2007 on the site of the original stadium of 1923. It has 90,000 seats, and its arch spans 315 metres.
model_hint: Wembley Stadium: the large stadium with a tall white arch over it, close up or from a distance. Not other stadiums.

name: The Churchill Arms
fact: There has been a pub here since 1824. Famous for its huge floral displays, it has been called London's most colourful pub, and it claims to have been the first London pub with a Thai restaurant.
notes: Pub: check it is still open before the field test. The name must be readable in the photo.
model_hint: The Churchill Arms: a corner pub covered in flowers and hanging baskets, with "Churchill Arms" on the front. The pub's own name must be readable; another pub, or a pub interior without the name, is not this item.

name: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese
fact: There has been a pub here since 1538. It was rebuilt shortly after the Great Fire of 1666, and Charles Dickens, G. K. Chesterton and Mark Twain were among its regulars.
notes: Pub: check it is still open before the field test. The name must be readable in the photo.
model_hint: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese: the old pub sign and lamp at the entrance of a narrow alley off Fleet Street. The pub's own name must be readable; another pub, or a pub interior without the name, is not this item.

name: The George Inn
fact: The George is the only surviving galleried coaching inn in London. It was rebuilt in 1677 after a fire, and Charles Dickens mentioned it in Little Dorrit.
notes: Pub: check it is still open before the field test. The name must be readable in the photo.
model_hint: The George Inn: a black-and-white galleried coaching inn around a cobbled yard, with "George Inn" on the sign. The pub's own name must be readable; another pub, or a pub interior without the name, is not this item.

name: The Blackfriar
fact: The Black Friar was built in about 1875 on the site of a medieval Dominican friary. When it was nearly demolished in the 1960s, a campaign led by the poet John Betjeman saved it.
notes: Coordinates from the pub's point on OpenStreetMap (27 Oct 2026). Pub: check it is still open before the field test. The name must be readable in the photo.
model_hint: The Blackfriar: a narrow wedge-shaped pub with a statue of a jolly monk over the door and "Blackfriar" on the front. The pub's own name must be readable; another pub, or a pub interior without the name, is not this item.

name: Lamb & Flag
fact: The Lamb and Flag became a pub in 1772. Its upstairs room once hosted bare-knuckle prize fights, which earned it the nickname "The Bucket of Blood".
notes: Pub: check it is still open before the field test. The name must be readable in the photo.
model_hint: Lamb & Flag: a small brick pub in an alley, with a lamb-and-flag sign. The pub's own name must be readable; another pub, or a pub interior without the name, is not this item.

name: Ye Olde Mitre
fact: Ye Olde Mitre hides in a narrow alley off Ely Place, on the site of the London palace where the Bishops of Ely lived from 1290 to 1772. The pub was rebuilt in about 1773.
notes: Pub: check it is still open before the field test. The name must be readable in the photo.
model_hint: Ye Olde Mitre: a small old pub in a narrow alley, with a lantern and a "Ye Olde Mitre" sign. The pub's own name must be readable; another pub, or a pub interior without the name, is not this item.

name: Shakespeare's Head
fact: A bust of William Shakespeare looks out from a window at the front of the pub. One of its hands is missing, damaged by a bomb in the Second World War.
notes: Pub: check it is still open before the field test. The name must be readable in the photo.
model_hint: Shakespeare's Head: a mock-Tudor pub with a bust of Shakespeare in a first-floor window and a portrait sign. The pub's own name must be readable; another pub, or a pub interior without the name, is not this item.

name: The Prospect of Whitby
fact: The Prospect of Whitby claims to stand on the site of the oldest riverside tavern, from around 1520. It was once known as the Devil's Tavern, and the painters Turner and Whistler both sketched views from it.
notes: Pub: check it is still open before the field test. The name must be readable in the photo.
model_hint: The Prospect of Whitby: an old riverside pub with "Prospect of Whitby" on the front, on a cobbled street. The pub's own name must be readable; another pub, or a pub interior without the name, is not this item.

name: The Mayflower
fact: In July 1620 the Mayflower ship took on 65 passengers at its home port of Rotherhithe. At low tide you can spot the ship's original 1620 mooring point by the pub.
notes: Pub: check it is still open before the field test. The name must be readable in the photo.
model_hint: The Mayflower: a small black-fronted riverside pub with a Mayflower ship sign. The pub's own name must be readable; another pub, or a pub interior without the name, is not this item.

name: The Spaniards Inn
fact: The Spaniards Inn is believed to have been built in 1585. It appears in Dickens's The Pickwick Papers and Bram Stoker's Dracula, and highwaymen probably used it to watch the road.
notes: Pub: check it is still open before the field test. The name must be readable in the photo.
model_hint: The Spaniards Inn: a white weatherboarded country-style inn by a narrow road, with "The Spaniards" on it. The pub's own name must be readable; another pub, or a pub interior without the name, is not this item.

name: Platform 9¾
fact: In the Harry Potter stories, the Hogwarts Express leaves King's Cross from Platform 9¾. Here a luggage trolley disappears into the wall; it moved to the new concourse when the station was renovated.
notes: The Harry Potter shop next to it sells pictures of it; vision must see the real wall and trolley.
model_hint: The Platform 9¾ sign on a brick wall with a luggage trolley half-way into the wall, at King's Cross station. Not the Harry Potter shop's goods.

name: Paddington Bear statue
fact: This bronze statue by Marcus Cornish was unveiled by Paddington's creator, Michael Bond, on 24 February 2000. Bond created Paddington Bear in 1958.
model_hint: The bronze statue of Paddington Bear (duffle coat, hat, suitcase) sitting on a plinth in a railway station. Not toys, soft toys or the painted Paddington statues from the 2014 trail.

name: Leadenhall Market
fact: Leadenhall Market stood in for the streets near the Leaky Cauldron and Diagon Alley in the film Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (2001). The market building is Grade II* listed.
model_hint: Leadenhall Market: an ornate Victorian covered market street with a painted iron-and-glass roof, cream and maroon colours.

name: Abbey Road zebra crossing
location: Abbey Road, St John's Wood, NW8, outside Abbey Road Studios
fact: The Beatles were photographed on this crossing on 8 August 1969 for the cover of their Abbey Road album. It was Grade II listed in December 2010.
notes: Live road: tell players to take the photo from the pavement.
model_hint: Black-and-white zebra crossing on Abbey Road outside Abbey Road Studios.

name: Earl's Court police box
location: Outside Earl's Court station, Earl's Court Road exit, SW5 9AA
fact: Installed in 1996 by the Metropolitan Police, based on Gilbert MacKenzie Trench's 1929 design. More were planned but this was the only one ever built.
notes: Still outside the station per visitor reviews dated May 2026. The council has been looking at moving it to the corner of Hogarth Road, close by; no decision found. Use a wide location radius and re-check before launch. Coordinates are the station's.
model_hint: Blue police box with POLICE BOX on the sign at the top, standing outside Earl's Court station. Not toys, models or other blue boxes.

name: Sherlock Holmes statue
location: Marylebone Road, outside Baker Street station, NW1
fact: This 3-metre statue by John Doubleday was unveiled in 1999. There was no room for it on Baker Street itself, so it stands outside Baker Street station, two blocks from the detective's fictional home at 221B.
model_hint: The bronze statue of Sherlock Holmes in a deerstalker and cape, holding a pipe, on a plinth by a busy road. Not the "221B" museum front or other statues.

name: Hope the blue whale
location: Natural History Museum, Cromwell Road, SW7
fact: Hope is the skeleton of a 25.2-metre blue whale stranded near Wexford, Ireland, in 1891. Since 2017 she has hung in Hintze Hall, diving towards visitors as they come in.
notes: Indoors: location may be imprecise. Postcards in the museum shop would pass the location check (open decision at step 5).
model_hint: The blue whale skeleton hanging in the great hall of the Natural History Museum. Not the old Diplodocus cast, other skeletons or toys.

name: V&A Rotunda Chandelier
fact: The glass chandelier in the V&A's entrance hall is by Dale Chihuly. The museum commissioned it in 1999, and it was enlarged in 2001 to the work that hangs there today, "Ice Blue and Spring Green".
notes: Indoors: location may be imprecise. Postcards in the museum shop would pass the location check (open decision at step 5).
model_hint: The large chandelier of blue and green twisted glass hanging in the V&A's domed entrance hall.

name: British Museum Great Court
location: British Museum, Great Russell Street, WC1
fact: The Great Court is the largest covered square in Europe. Its roof uses 1,656 pairs of glass panes, each a unique shape, and it was opened by Queen Elizabeth II in 2000.
notes: Indoors: location may be imprecise. Postcards in the museum shop would pass the location check (open decision at step 5).
model_hint: The British Museum Great Court: a white courtyard under a curved roof of triangular glass panes, around the round Reading Room.

name: Tate Modern
fact: Tate Modern is in the former Bankside Power Station, designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, with a 99-metre chimney. It opened in 2000, and entry to the collection is free.
notes: The Turbine Hall is indoors: location may be imprecise.
model_hint: Tate Modern: the brick former power station with its tall central chimney, or its huge Turbine Hall inside.

name: Belisha beacon
fact: Named after Transport Minister Leslie Hore-Belisha, who added the beacons to pedestrian crossings in 1934, starting in London.
model_hint: Amber globe lamp on top of a black-and-white striped pole beside a zebra crossing. Not traffic lights or other orange lamps.

name: Westminster street sign
fact: The white sign with black lettering and a red postcode was designed in 1967 by Sir Misha Black's Design Research Unit.
notes: Must read CITY OF WESTMINSTER on the sign. One V&A record gives 1976; most sources say 1967.
model_hint: White street-name sign with black capital letters, a red postcode district and the words CITY OF WESTMINSTER. Not street signs from other boroughs.

name: Green cabmen's shelter
fact: 61 of these green huts were built for cab drivers by the Cabmen's Shelter Fund, founded in 1875. Only 13 survive and all are Grade II listed.
model_hint: Small green wooden hut with a pitched roof, standing on a London street or in the road. Not garden sheds, newspaper kiosks or other green huts.

name: City of London dragon
fact: The silver boundary dragons are modelled on two statues saved from the demolished Coal Exchange and re-erected on Victoria Embankment in 1963.
notes: Sources disagree on the total (10 to 14); do not state a number in the app.
model_hint: Silver or painted metal dragon standing on a plinth, holding a shield with a red cross on white. Not other dragons, flags or decorations.

name: Overground roundel
fact: Each TfL service has its own roundel colour; the Overground's is orange.
model_hint: TfL roundel with an orange ring and a blue bar across it. Not roundels in other colours and not round logos of other brands.

name: Elizabeth line roundel
fact: The purple roundel was designed to stand apart from the Underground's red and the Overground's orange.
model_hint: TfL roundel with a purple ring and a blue bar across it. Not roundels in other colours and not round logos of other brands.

name: Bus stop roundel
fact: Buses have their own red-and-white version of the roundel.
model_hint: TfL roundel on a London bus stop sign. Not roundels at stations and not round logos of other brands.

name: River roundel
fact: London's river services use a blue version of the roundel.
notes: Look for the word River on the bar.
model_hint: TfL roundel with a blue ring, used for river services at Thames piers. Not roundels in other colours and not round logos of other brands.

name: Leslie Green station
fact: Architect Leslie Green was appointed in 1903 and gave dozens of new Tube stations their ox-blood red tiled fronts. He died in 1908, aged 33.
notes: Examples: Russell Square, Chalk Farm, Belsize Park. Street-level exterior, so no ticket needed.
model_hint: Tube station front covered in ox-blood red glazed tiles, with large semicircular windows on the upper floor. Not ordinary red brick buildings or red-painted shopfronts.

name: Labyrinth artwork
fact: Artist Mark Wallinger made 270 different labyrinths in 2013, one for every Tube station, to mark the Underground's 150th anniversary.
notes: Position varies by station; some are beyond the ticket barriers. No GPS underground.
model_hint: Square white enamel panel showing a single-path labyrinth in black lines with a red X at the entrance, mounted in a Tube station. Not maps, mazes on posters or other artworks.

name: Frank Pick memorial
fact: Unveiled on 7 November 2016, the 75th anniversary of the death of Frank Pick, the man behind the roundel and the Johnston typeface. Made by artists Langlands & Bell.
notes: In the station entrance, before the ticket barriers (PhotoHound guide), so no ticket needed. Station coordinates, for the map only. No GPS underground: verify by image and the words Frank Pick.
model_hint: A long marble wall in the Piccadilly Circus ticket hall with bronze words (BEAUTY < IMMORTALITY, UTILITY < PERFECTION, GOODNESS < RIGHTEOUSNESS, TRUTH < WISDOM) beside a roundel whose bar reads FRANK PICK. If the bar reads FRANK PICK, choose this item, not the Underground roundel.

name: Sherlock Holmes tiles
location: Baker Street station, Bakerloo and Jubilee line platforms
fact: The Sherlock Holmes silhouette tiles were designed by Michael Douglas and added when the station was refurbished in the 1980s.
notes: Station coordinates, for the map only. Inside the paid area; no GPS. Only paid-area item in the set.
model_hint: Glazed tiles fixed to an Underground platform wall at Baker Street, showing the silhouette of Sherlock Holmes in a deerstalker hat with a pipe. Only the platform tiles count. Not merchandise, posters, printed signs, shop displays, statues or any other Sherlock Holmes image.

name: Aldwych closed station
fact: Opened in 1907 as Strand station and closed on 30 September 1994. It is now used for filming and for London Transport Museum's Hidden London tours.
notes: Street frontage only.
model_hint: Ox-blood red tiled front of the closed Aldwych (originally Strand) station on the Strand.

name: Jimi Hendrix
fact: The guitarist lived here in 1968 and 1969. His plaque sits next door to Handel's, one of London's best-known plaque pairings.
model_hint: Round blue plaque naming Jimi Hendrix.

name: George Frideric Handel
fact: The composer lived here from 1723 until his death in 1759, and wrote Messiah in this house.
model_hint: Round blue plaque naming George Frideric Handel.

name: John Lennon
fact: Lennon lived here for about five months in 1968. The plaque went up in 2010.
model_hint: Round blue plaque naming John Lennon.

name: Ada Lovelace
location: 12 St James's Square, St James's, SW1Y 4RB
fact: The plaque calls her a pioneer of computing. She lived here from 1837 to 1846.
notes: Plaque is behind railings.
model_hint: Round blue plaque naming Ada, Countess of Lovelace.

name: Isaac Newton
fact: Newton's house was demolished, so the 1908 plaque was fixed to the new building in 1915.
model_hint: Round blue plaque naming Sir Isaac Newton.

name: Karl Marx
fact: Marx lived here from 1851 to 1856 in a few cramped rooms while working on Das Kapital.
notes: Plaque is on the second floor, above a restaurant.
model_hint: Round blue plaque naming Karl Marx.

name: John Logie Baird
fact: Baird gave the first demonstration of television in this building in January 1926.
notes: Several other Baird plaques are nearby; match the address.
model_hint: Round blue plaque naming John Logie Baird and the first demonstration of television.

name: Charles Dickens
fact: Dickens lived here from 1837 to 1839 and wrote Oliver Twist in the house, which is now the Charles Dickens Museum.
model_hint: Round blue plaque naming Charles Dickens.

name: Virginia Woolf
fact: Woolf lived here from 1907 to 1911. George Bernard Shaw, an earlier tenant, has a plaque on the same house.
notes: Postcode taken from the Woolf page; the Shaw page for the same house gives W1T 6LQ.
model_hint: Round blue plaque naming Virginia Woolf. The same house has a plaque for George Bernard Shaw, which is not this item.

name: Charles Darwin
location: UCL Biological Sciences Building, Gower Street, Bloomsbury, WC1E 6BT
fact: Darwin lived in a house on this site from 1838 to 1842. The house is gone and a university building stands in its place.
notes: Coordinates from the Historical Marker Database, not English Heritage.
model_hint: Round blue plaque naming Charles Darwin.

name: VR
fact: Queen Victoria, who reigned from 1837 to 1901.
notes: Some early Victorian boxes carry no cypher at all.
model_hint: Royal cypher on a post box: the letters V R, usually below a crown. Only on a post box.

name: EVIIR
fact: King Edward VII, who reigned from 1901 to 1910.
model_hint: Royal cypher on a post box: E VII R (two Is), usually below a crown. Easily confused with E VIII R. Only on a post box.

name: GR
fact: King George V, who reigned from 1910 to 1936.
model_hint: Royal cypher on a post box: G R with no numeral, usually below a crown. If VI appears between the letters, this is G VI R instead. Only on a post box.

name: EVIIIR
fact: King Edward VIII reigned for only 326 days in 1936, so very few boxes carry his cypher.
notes: Nearest one to central London reported on The Highway, Wapping E1 (one 2015 blog source, not re-confirmed). About two dozen estimated across London, mostly in outer areas.
model_hint: Royal cypher on a post box: E VIII R (three Is). Very rare and easily confused with E VII R (two Is); if you cannot count three Is clearly, do not choose this. Only on a post box.

name: GVIR
fact: King George VI, who reigned from 1936 to 1952.
model_hint: Royal cypher on a post box: G VI R, usually below a crown. Only on a post box.

name: EIIR
fact: Queen Elizabeth II, who reigned from 1952 to 2022.
model_hint: Royal cypher on a post box: E II R, usually below a crown. Only on a post box.

name: CIIIR
fact: King Charles III, on the throne since 2022. The newest cypher.
model_hint: Royal cypher on a post box: C III R, below a crown. Found on the newest boxes. Only on a post box.
